newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire and Rwanda clash across border.
newsitem.headline: Zaire and Rwanda clash across border.

text.p: Zairean and Rwandan forces traded mortar and machinegun fire across their border on Tuesday as the U.N. sought satellite photos to help trace hundreds of thousands of Hutu refugees fleeing Tutsi rebels inside Zaire.

Reuters reporters and other witnesses in the Rwandan border town of Cyangugu, just across the border from Bukavu, spoke of exchanges lasting about two hours. Aid workers at one stage had to take refuge from the firing, they said.
"It was a fairly sustained bombardment," Reuters Television producer Tony Wende said. "The Rwandans fired mortars, anti-aircraft guns and heavy machine-guns with tracers."
The exchange appeared to be the most serious since one in late September, aid officials said.

Earlier, Zaire's sick and absent president sought to reassert his authority in the east of his country by placing it under military rule and his interior minister accused Rwanda's Tutsi-led government of trying to carve out a Tutsi empire.
A spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees said in Geneva the agency had no access to up to 400,000 Rwandan Hutus around Goma and 300,000 in Uvira and Bukavu to the south.
"We have requested governments to give us satellite information," Augustine Mahiga, regional coordinator, said. "Our primary concern now is to avert a humanitarian catastrophy."
In Brussels, the European Union's aid commissioner Emma Bonino said one million people, many of them already refugees from Rwanda and Burundi, could die in Zaire.
The conflict between Zairean troops and Tutsi Banyamulenge rebels inside Zaire threatens to drag in neighbouring Rwanda and Burundi and some say it could presage the breakup of Zaire.
A government spokesman in Kinshasa said President Mobutu Sese Seko had placed South and North Kivu under military rule. Mobutu is in Switzerland receiving prostate cancer treatment.
Interior Minister Kamanda wa Kamanda told Belgian RTBF radio Rwanda wanted to create a greater Tutsi-land. "They want to drive into the interior all those considered non-Tutsis."
Underlying the violence is the Hutu-Tutsi rivalry that exploded in the 1994 massacres in Rwanda of up to a million Tutsis and pro-opposition Hutus by hardline Hutus.
Ethnic tension in eastern Zaire degenerated into clashes after the arrival of more than a million Rwandan Hutu refugees in 1994. Hutus from Burundi also fled into the same region.
Each side in the Zaire fighting, which began around Uvira near the Burundi border on October 18, accuses the other of having military support from Rwandans.
Refugees say the Uvira death toll runs into hundreds.
Independent reports suggest that Hutu soldiers from the former Rwandan army which joined in the 1994 genocide are fighting alongside Zairean troops.
A nurse in a Bukavu hospital told Reuters three former Rwandan Hutu soldiers were treated for wounds sustained in fighting against the rebels at Kaziba south of Bukavu.
The Banyamulenge say they are fighting Zairean attempts to expel them. Zaire accuses Rwanda of fighting alongside them.
Despite the upheaval in eastern Zaire, Rwandan Hutus are reluctant to go home, where they fear reprisals.
